## Introduction

This document describes a novel Bayesian approach to jointly model scoring and ranking data using the \texttt{inlajoint} package [@rustand_fast_2024]. While a frequentist approach to joint modelling already exists in the form of the Mallows-Binomial model [@pearce_unified_2022], a Bayesian model has yet to be proposed in this context. We define and describe this novel Bayesian model. Then, we apply it on the Gallo et al. [-@gallo_new_2023] dataset and report the results it provides. Finally, we discuss the model's limitations and the further work necessary to validate it for use in real-world scenarios. During the model fitting, we provide all code necessary to reproduce the analyses performed in this document.

## Model Definition

To unify the scale of the scoring and ranking data, we first transform the data through z-scoring as follows:
\begin{gather*}
y^{z}_{i,j} = \frac{y_{ij} - \hat{\bar{y}}}{\hat{\sigma}_y} \\
r^{z}_{i,j} = \frac{r_{ij} - \hat{\bar{r}}}{\hat{\sigma}_r}
\end{gather*}
Using the standardised $y^{z}_{i,j}$ data, we modify the Bayesian hierarchical model for scores defined by Heyard et al. [-@heyard_rethinking_2022] in order to obtain:
\begin{gather*}
y^{z}_{i,j} = \beta_0^y + \theta^{y}_{i} + \lambda^{y}_{j} \\
\theta^{y} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\theta^y}^2) \quad \quad \beta_0^y \sim N(\mu^y, \sigma_y^2)
\end{gather*}
where $\theta^{y}_{i}$ represents the latent qualities of an object $o_i$ according to the transformed scoring data, $\lambda^{y}_{j}$ represents the assessor-specific differences in strictness and scoring habit, and $\beta_0^y$ represents and estimates the mean standardised score of all objects. 

Analogously, we create a second model for the transformed ranking data as follows:
\begin{gather*}
y^{z}_{i,j} = \beta_0^y + \theta^{r}_{i} \\
\theta^{r} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\theta^r}^2) \quad \quad \beta_0^r \sim N(\mu^r, \sigma_r^2)
\end{gather*}
where $\theta^{r}_{i}$ represents the latent qualities of an object $o_i$ according to the transformed ranking data, and $\beta_0^r$ represents and estimates the mean standardised rank of all objects. 

We join these models by defining a correlation constraint ($\text{corr}(\theta^{y},  \theta^{r}) = \rho_{\theta}$) between the random effects of both models, which are effectively the latent quality variables. The \texttt{inlajoint} package does this automatically, and fits both models simultaneously taking this correlation into account. This provides the final model:
\begin{gather*}
\begin{cases}
    y^{z}_{i,j} = \beta_0^y + \theta^{y}_{i} + \lambda^{y}_{j}  \\
    r^{z}_{i,j} = \beta_0^r + \theta^{r}_{i} 
\end{cases} \\
\theta^{y} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\theta^y}^2) \quad \quad  \theta^{r} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\theta^r}^2)  \\
\text{corr}(\theta^{y},  \theta^{r}) = \rho_{\theta} \\
\beta_0^y \sim N(\mu^y, \sigma_y^2) \quad \quad \beta_0^y \sim N(\mu^r, \sigma_r^2) 
\end{gather*}

## Model Fitting & Results
In the Gallo et al. dataset, there are 259 scoring observations, but only 49 ranking observations. This provides us with three paths for model fitting: (1) We analyse the data as-is and ignore the missingness of the ranking data. (2) We analyse only the complete cases in the data and remove 210 scoring observations. (3) We correct for the difference in the amount of observations in the model. While path (3) is the most promising for real-world applications, it is beyond the scope of this thesis. We therefore only provide examples of models fitted using path (1) and path (2).  

\newpage

### As-is Analysis

The code below was used to fit the joint model:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(INLA)
library(INLAjoint)
source("../code/0.3_plotting_functions.R")

```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

# Importing scoring and ranking data
dat_scores <- read.csv("../data/clean/scores_long.csv")
dat_ranks <- read.csv("../data/clean/rank_full_long.csv")

# Joining scores and ranks
dat_joint <- dat_scores
dat_joint$value_rank <- rep(NA, 280)
dat_joint$value_rank[dat_joint$RandomRevID %in% unique(dat_ranks$RandomRevID)] <-
  dat_ranks$value

#Substituting grant_id for INLA joint
dat_joint$grant_id <- as.numeric(gsub('x', replacement =  "", dat_joint$grant_id))

# Only select complete cases
dat_as_is <- dat_joint
dat_c_cases <- dat_joint[complete.cases(dat_joint),] 

# Standardising everything
dat_as_is$std_score <- round((dat_as_is$value - mean(dat_as_is$value, na.rm = T)) / sd(dat_as_is$value, na.rm = T),3)
dat_as_is$std_rank  <- round((dat_as_is$value_rank - mean(dat_as_is$value_rank, na.rm = T)) / sd(dat_as_is$value_rank, na.rm = T), 3)

dat_as_is <- dat_as_is[, c(1,2,5,6)]

# Standardising everything
dat_c_cases$std_score <- round((dat_c_cases$value - mean(dat_c_cases$value)) / sd(dat_c_cases$value),3)
dat_c_cases$std_rank  <- round((dat_c_cases$value_rank - mean(dat_c_cases$value_rank)) / sd(dat_c_cases$value_rank),3)

dat_c_cases <- dat_c_cases[, c(1,2,5,6)]

```

```{r}
#| warning: false


# Overview of data
kable(head(dat_as_is))

# Fitting model
inla_sr_joint_as_is <- joint(
  formLong = list(
    std_score  ~ 1 + (1 | grant_id) + (1| RandomRevID),
    std_rank  ~ 1 + (1 | grant_id) 
  ),
  dataLong = dat_as_is, id = "grant_id",
  family  = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
  corLong = T   
)

```

The resulting posterior mean estimates of the 10 best objects' latent qualities in the as-is model are presented in the table below:


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

res_is <- inla_sr_joint_as_is$summary.random$IDIntercept_L1$mean
grant_id <- unique(dat_scores$grant_id)

dat_is <- as.data.frame(cbind(grant_id, res_is))[1:28,]
dat_is$res_is <- as.numeric(dat_is$res_is)
dat_is <- dat_is[order(dat_is$res_is, decreasing = F),]

final_res_is <- dat_is[1:10,]

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

final_res_is$res_is <- round(final_res_is$res_is,2)
res_is_table <- as.data.frame(t(final_res_is))
colnames(res_is_table) <- final_res_is$grant_id
rownames(res_is_table) <- c("", "Estimate")
res_is_table <- res_is_table[-1,]

kable(res_is_table)

```

### Complete Cases

The code below was used to fit the joint model:

```{r}
#| warning: false


# Overview of data
kable(head(dat_c_cases))

# Fitting model
inla_sr_joint_complete <- joint(
  formLong = list(
    std_score  ~ 1 + (1 | grant_id) + (1| RandomRevID),
    std_rank  ~ 1 + (1 | grant_id) 
  ),
  dataLong = dat_c_cases, id = "grant_id",
  family  = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
  corLong = T   
)


```

The resulting posterior mean estimates of the 10 best objects' latent qualities in the complete cases model are presented in the table below:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

res_complete <- inla_sr_joint_complete$summary.random$IDIntercept_L1$mean[1:11]
grant_id <- unique(dat_c_cases$grant_id)


dat_complete <- as.data.frame(cbind(grant_id, res_complete))
dat_complete$res_complete <- as.numeric(dat_complete$res_complete)
dat_complete <- dat_complete[order(dat_complete$res_complete, decreasing = F),]

final_res_complete <- dat_complete[1:10,]

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

final_res_complete$res_complete <- round(final_res_complete$res_complete,2)
final_res_complete$grant_id <- paste0("x", final_res_complete$grant_id)
res_complete_table <- as.data.frame(t(final_res_complete))
colnames(res_complete_table) <- final_res_complete$grant_id
rownames(res_complete_table) <- c("", "Estimate")
res_complete_table <- res_complete_table[-1,]

kable(res_complete_table)

```

## Discussion and Limitations

In this supplement, we present how the \texttt{inlajoint} package can be used in combination with scoring and ranking data to create a joint model assessing grant proposal qualities. While this model is still in its early stages, we provide all code snippets necessary to use, reproduce, and extend it.  

Much work still remains to be done before this joint model can be used in practice. First of all, in our model definition, we transform the ranking data using z-scoring. Performing such transformations on ranking data is a polarising topic in the literature [@stevens_theory_1946; @mosteller_data_1977; @velleman_nominal_1993]. Whether this can be avoided, and what other possible model formulations exist still needs to be clarified. Then, due to the nature of grant proposal review datasets, it is very likely that real world datasets will have many missing data points. Giving rankings to objects is a cumbersome task, and in consequence only partial ranking data will be available in most real-world scenarios. Strategies to deal with incomplete data also need to be investigated. Finally, the \texttt{inlajoint} package is very flexible, and many options exist to define the correlation structure of the model. These options should also be explored when creating a joint model.      

Future work on this model could compare the Bayesian joint approach presented in this supplement to other already existing models used to analyse scoring and ranking data. Moreover, analysis on simulation data could be used to validate and quantify the performance of this model. While the work presented in this supplement is only preliminary, it can serve as a stepping stone for further work in implementing such joint models in the assessment of grant proposal qualities.
